title: TS2322: Excess Property Checks on Object Literals
symptoms: Type error: Type '{ ... }' has no properties in common with type or Object literal may only specify known properties.
roast: Trying to craft armor by stuffing an apple into the crafting grid: TypeScript rejects unknown ingredients.
diagnosis: TypeScript performs Excess Property Checking when object literals are assigned directly to typed variables or passed as function arguments, rejecting unmodeled properties.
debuggingSteps: Add the property to the interface/type definition if it is genuinely part of the model
Add an index signature [key: string]: unknown if dynamic properties are permissible
Pass through an intermediate variable to bypass excess check if intended
whyItWorks: Declaring 'age?: number' informs the TypeScript type checker that the age property is an authorized optional field.
tests: interface U { name: string; age?: number; } const u: U = { name: 'A', age: 20 }; assert.strictEqual(u.name, 'A');

title: Unsound 'any' Bypass Causing Unchecked Runtime Crashes
symptoms: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined at runtime despite code compiling with zero TypeScript errors.
roast: Turning off mob griefing on your server and wondering why creepers still blow up in hardcore mode.
diagnosis: 'any' disables the TypeScript compiler's safety checks completely. Passing incorrect shapes across an 'any' boundary silences compile-time detection.
debuggingSteps: Replace 'any' with 'unknown' for untyped API responses or payloads
Use type guards or zod/valibot schema parsers before property access
Enable 'noImplicitAny' in tsconfig.json
whyItWorks: Using typed interfaces with optional chaining informs the compiler of possible nullish shapes and guarantees fallback handling.

title: Discriminated Union Type Narrowing Failure from Missing Guard
symptoms: TS2339: Property 'payload' does not exist on type 'SuccessAction | ErrorAction'.
roast: Attacking an Enderman with water while expecting it not to teleport: check its identity first.
diagnosis: TypeScript requires checking the discriminator tag (e.g. action.type) within a conditional block to narrow the union to a specific variant.
debuggingSteps: Add a switch (action.type) or if (action.type === '...') block
Ensure all union variants share a literal discriminant property
Use exhaustive matching with 'never' type in default cases
whyItWorks: Checking action.type === 'success' allows the compiler control-flow analysis to narrow action to the Success variant where 'data' is guaranteed.
tests: const a: Action = { type: 'success', data: 'ok' }; if (a.type === 'success') assert.strictEqual(a.data, 'ok');

title: TS2345: Optional Chaining Passing Undefined to Non-Nullable Parameter
symptoms: TS2345: Argument of type 'string | undefined' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string'.
roast: Giving a villager an empty invisible hand and expecting emerald trades: you handed him undefined.
diagnosis: Optional chaining (?.) returns 'undefined' if any parent property is null or undefined. Passing that expression to a function requiring a non-nullable type causes TS2345.
debuggingSteps: Provide a nullish coalescing default value: user?.name ?? 'Anonymous'
Or wrap the invocation in an if (user?.name) guard
Audit parameter signatures for nullability requirements
whyItWorks: Nullish coalescing (??) guarantees a non-null string fallback if user?.name evaluates to null or undefined.
tests: function g(n: string) { return n; } assert.strictEqual(g(undefined ?? 'def'), 'def');

title: TS2542: Index Signature in Type ReadonlyArray Only Permits Reading
symptoms: TS2542: Index signature in type 'readonly number[]' only permits reading.
roast: Trying to carve runes into bedrock: it's marked readonly for a reason.
diagnosis: ReadonlyArray<T> or readonly T[] removes mutable array methods (push, pop, splice) and marks indices read-only. Attempting to assign or push triggers compile-time errors.
debuggingSteps: Use non-mutating operations like .concat(), spread [...arr, item], or .slice()
Remove 'readonly' if the function is intentionally designed to mutate the array
Return a new array rather than mutating inputs
whyItWorks: Spreading the readonly array into a new mutable array produces a new array instance without violating the input's readonly immutability guarantee.
tests: const r: readonly number[] = [1]; const res = [...r, 2]; assert.deepStrictEqual(res, [1, 2]);

title: Blind Type Assertion 'as unknown as Target' Masking Schema Divergence
symptoms: Downstream code crashes with 'undefined is not a function' because the actual runtime JSON structure did not match the asserted type.
roast: Slapping a Netherite texture on a wooden shovel: it looks shiny until you hit an obsidian block and it shatters.
diagnosis: Type assertions ('as T') do not perform any runtime validation; they merely silence the compiler. If API payloads drift, the asserted type creates a false sense of security.
debuggingSteps: Use runtime schema parsing with libraries like Zod or custom type predicates (isTarget(x))
Validate required properties before casting
Avoid chaining 'as unknown as T' as an escape hatch
whyItWorks: User-defined type guards ('obj is ApiResponse') verify actual runtime properties before allowing TypeScript to narrow the type safely.
tests: function isU(o: any): o is { id: string } { return Boolean(o?.id); } assert.strictEqual(isU({ id: '1' }), true);

title: Numeric Enum Reverse Mapping Generating Unexpected Object Keys
symptoms: Object.keys(StatusEnum) contains both strings and numbers, doubling the expected length.
roast: Opening a dispenser and getting twice as many arrows as you put in, half of which are labeled with upside-down numbers.
diagnosis: TypeScript compiles numeric enums with reverse mappings: Status[0] = 'Pending' and Status['Pending'] = 0. Object.keys() returns both sets of keys.
debuggingSteps: Use string enums (enum Status { Pending = 'PENDING' }) which do not emit reverse mappings
Or prefer const object literals: const Status = { Pending: 'pending' } as const
Filter numeric keys when iterating numeric enums
whyItWorks: 'as const' object literals emit clean JavaScript objects without synthetic numeric reverse mappings.
tests: const S = { A: 'a' } as const; assert.deepStrictEqual(Object.keys(S), ['A']);

sources.title: TypeScript Handbook - Enums and Reverse Mapping

title: TS2339: Property Does Not Exist on Unconstrained Generic Type T
symptoms: TS2339: Property 'id' does not exist on type 'T' inside a generic function.
roast: Telling a generic crafting table to craft without specifying any recipe blueprints: what is 'T' supposed to be?
diagnosis: An unconstrained generic <T> can be any type (number, boolean, null, undefined). Accessing specific properties like item.id requires constraining T.
debuggingSteps: Add a generic constraint with 'extends': <T extends { id: string }>
Define an interface for the required shape: <T extends HasId>
Verify caller arguments fulfill the constraint contract
whyItWorks: The 'extends HasId' constraint proves to the compiler that every permissible substitution of T will contain an 'id: string' property.
tests: function getId<T extends { id: string }>(x: T) { return x.id; } assert.strictEqual(getId({ id: '123' }), '123');

title: Unchecked Undefined Access on Record/Index Signature Types
symptoms: TypeScript assumes dict[key] is always present (type string), but at runtime it returns undefined and throws TypeError.
roast: Looking for cake in an empty chest without checking if the chest has items: surprise, it's air.
diagnosis: By default, TypeScript treats Record<string, string>[key] as 'string'. If the key doesn't exist, runtime returns undefined without compiler warning unless noUncheckedIndexedAccess is enabled.
debuggingSteps: Enable 'noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true' in tsconfig.json compilerOptions
Explicitly type records with undefined: Record<string, string | undefined>
Check presence before use: if (key in dict) or dict[key] !== undefined
badExample:
const dict: Record<string, string> = {};
const upper = dict["missing"].toUpperCase(); // Compiles fine, crashes at runtime!
fixedExample:
const dict: Record<string, string | undefined> = {};
const upper = dict["missing"]?.toUpperCase() ?? "DEFAULT";
whyItWorks: Typing values as 'string | undefined' forces callers to handle the absent key case with optional chaining or default guards.
tests: const d: Record<string, string | undefined> = {}; assert.strictEqual(d['a']?.toUpperCase() ?? 'DEF', 'DEF');

title: Key Type Widening from Object.keys() to string[]
symptoms: TS7053: Element implicitly has an 'any' type because type 'string' can't be used to index type 'Config'.
roast: Labeling your chest slots with infinite string names and wondering why the 3-slot inventory rejects them.
diagnosis: Object.keys(obj) returns string[] rather than (keyof typeof obj)[], because JavaScript objects can have additional runtime properties added at prototype level.
debuggingSteps: Cast keys safely: (Object.keys(obj) as (keyof typeof obj)[])
Use Object.entries() with typed tuple destructuring
Define a typedKeys helper function
whyItWorks: Casting to (keyof Config)[] refines the key type from broad string down to the exact union ('port' | 'host'), permitting safe indexing.
tests: const o = { a: 1 }; (Object.keys(o) as (keyof typeof o)[]).forEach(k => assert.strictEqual(o[k], 1));
